speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the House rose at one o'clock, the Hon. Member for Peace River (Mr. Cooper) had the floor.

Mr. Speaker, when I finished at one o'clock, I had just given a brief overview of the Accord from the perspective of an Albertan and tried to relate some of the concerns that I thought Albertans might have with the Accord and to address some of the concerns we may have
as to the impact it would have on our particular province. In the few minutes that I have left, I want to talk a bit about the process and I want to touch finally on the future of the constitutional process.
It was not uncommon, as we went through the constitutional hearings, to hear criticisms of the method used to bring about the Meech Lake Accord. People were critical of this so-called marathon negotiation, these in camera meetings. The implications of that, of course, were that Canadians were shut out of the negotiation process, did not know what was going on and therefore were not legitimately represented at the table.
I want to speak to that criticism because I think it is important that Canadians understand that this process is probably the only process that would have allowed us to get this agreement. It is very simple. The reason the agreement came together was that in marathon negotiations, people do not have an opportunity to walk out. They do not have an opportunity to change their minds, to go off and think about all sorts of things that might distract them from the issues before them. They are also under a lot of pressure to sit at the table, work out a compromise, work out a deal with which everyone can live. I feel it is absolutely essential that that type of marathon negotiation be used in all sorts of difficult consultations such as that which we had at Meech Lake Accord.
The other thing I want to talk about very quickly is this problem of in camera meetings. I find it really difficult to understand why the Prime Minister particularly would be criticized for holding these meetings in camera. We do this in all parts of our lives. We do it in business, we do it in day-today existence, we do it in all sorts of negotiations. The reason we do it in camera is that we do not want people playing to the audience, playing to the cameras. We want them to disucss seriously the issues before them. I think that was a major factor in bringing about this unanimous accord on the Meech Lake that no one thought was possible.
I feel that that process was the right one and it is one that should not be criticized. In fact, I would go even further. I would say that if more of this type of approach had been used in the aboriginal conferences on Indian self-government, we would then have had a better chance for a deal. I would advocate that in future negotiations this type of process be considered and, where possible, utilized.
The last point I want to touch on is the future process for constitutional reform. As you are aware, after hearing all of the evidence and studying the past process and that which we anticipate for the future, the committee recommended that there be established a joint Senate and House of Commons committee, the mandate of which would be to hold public
October 1, 1987

hearings on constitutional issues. It would examine the evidence arising from the various issues before it and would have an opportunity to study the implications of each of these issues. It would, of course, allow public participation, public debate, and public input into the constitutional matter which is on the agenda of the First Ministers. The committee would do the ground work for the First Ministers in a very public way before the First Ministers met for final negotiations.
I obviously support this proposal. However, Mr. John Holtby appeared before the committee and made a proposal which I think is the father of the committee's recommendation. He recommended a committee process and went one step further. He recommended that the committee be made up of members of the various legislatures across Canada, federal as well as provincial and territorial.
It was a radical approach and I am sure it caused some concerns because of its newness. Even though the committee has recommended a joint House of Commons and Senate committee, 1 think the Holtby proposal deserves future consideration. The advantage of it would be that we would draw in all levels of Government and give them the opportunity to discuss the issues. In that way we would get a national perspective rather than a provincial or territorial approach to the issues.
There are a number of issues which will have to be dealt with in the future. I do not have much time so I will merely outline them. One issue which I spent a lot of time discussing in my remarks prior to one o'clock is that of Senate reform. The concerns which were demonstrated by the women's groups which appeared before the committee must be addressed at a First Ministers' conference. Aboriginal rights and the issue of self-government must be addressed. Effort must be put into the definition of self-government. Effort must be made to reach a compromise in order to bring about agreement in that important constitutional area.
In conclusion, I really do believe that the evidence which was put before the committee studying the Meech Lake Accord showed that the Accord is in fact a seamless web. It is a very delicate fabric. Due to that there is, at this time, no room for amendment. That does not preclude future discussions, nor does it preclude First Ministers making important decisions on important issues. However, it does mean that the Meech Lake Accord must proceed in the form in which it exists today.
I think this agreement is good for my Province of Alberta. It is good for Canada. It is a document which Canadians can be very proud of. It will serve as a fundamental document for the future of constitutional amendments and process in this nation.

Mr. Speaker, I listened to the Member's remarks with great interest. I thank him for the solicitous manner in which he addressed the situation of Quebec in the Constitution. He said that it was important to reach this agreement because with Quebec outside, Ontario had a sole
Constitution Amendment, 1987
veto. The argument put to Canadians was that we had to do everything necessary to get Quebec to sign this agreement.
This ignores the fact that although the Quebec Government did not sign the agreement in 1981, Quebec was not outside the agreement. There were probably 70 Members of Parliament from Quebec who voted for the agreement. In order to get the agreement of the Quebec Government we did not have to agree to anything. Every single item in the Meech Lake Accord was not necessary to get the agreement of the present Government of Quebec.
I want to ask the Member about Senate reform. Does he think that Senate reform is realistic with the requirement of unanimity now that the provincial Premiers will be proposing lists from which Senators will be named?
The Member said that Albertans now have a veto on Senate reform. That was the proposition put to Israel Asper in the constitutional committee by the Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan). Mr. Asper said:
Yes, that is true. Meech gives Manitoba a veto. It is a veto we do not want.
We want an amending formula that is truly workable. Seven provinces
representing 50 per cent of the population is-
-truly workable, he suggested. He went on to argue that we have years of history in this country which suggest that we will not get unanimity, that we are putting ourselves into a constitutional straitjacket, and that Senate reform will be a dead issue. Would the Member care to respond to these concerns?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the Member's comments and questions. First, with regard to Quebec being involved in the Constitution at the moment, I was careful in my remarks to say that Quebec is legally and technically part of the Constitution of Canada right now. That is not disputed.
The problem, which I think is well accepted by Canadians, is that by the spirit of the Constitution Quebec has not considered itself a participant. The best example of that of which I know is the most recent round of constitutional negotiations on aboriginal rights. Quebec sat in on them but did not view itself as having a vote or being a participant. As a result of that Quebec has not been a participant in the spirit of the Constitution. I think that is what the Meech Lake Accord is trying to achieve. It wants not only the legal and technical participation of Quebec but wants to bring Quebec in, in a spiritual sense, which I think is much needed in Canada.
On the issue of Senate reform the Member asked whether Senate reform is realistic after the Meech Lake Accord. He asked whether it is possible to get a compromise and what kind of impact will result from the Premiers having the opportunity to name Senators.
I believe with all my heart that Senate reform is still a realistic option. Not only is it a realistic option, I think it is a necessary option for the maturing of our country and the healing of some of the wounds which exist between the

October 1, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
different regions in the nation. I think it is rightly placed as an item of high priority for the First Ministers.
Mr. Asper, when appearing before the committee, responded to the issue of a veto. As I said earlier, a number of witnesses appeared who had different perspectives on different things. The beauty of the veto which Alberta and Manitoba now have on issues such as Senate reform is that when every player at the table has a veto they also have a lever with which they can apply pressure for a compromise. That is a lever that Manitoba and Alberta never had before. I think that is essential and one of the things that gives us a better chance for Senate reform.

Mr. Speaker, I suggest to the Hon. Member that he is ignoring at least 50 years of constitutional history in this country, because it was felt for at least that period of time that we could not patriate our Constitution if we did not have the agreement of the provinces and the federal Government.
Certainly that was the assumption under which people were working for a long time, until the previous Government decided in 1980 to put forward a proposal, with the support of only two of the provinces. It was impossible to get the agreement of all the provinces on an amending formula and charter of rights. For years we struggled over the question of an amending formula.
I suggest that the Premiers at that time had that kind of practical veto. They could have compromised but did not, and 50 years went by when we were unable to make progress and get unanimous agreement on an amending formula.
It is fine for the Member to say that because of some perceived good will we will get unanimous agreement in the future, but is that the kind of situation we should leave for the future of this country and its Constitution? Is that the kind of straitjacket we should put on ourselves?
Let us face it, none of the provinces gave up anything in this agreement. There was no give and take between the provinces. All of the provinces received something and only the federal Government gave something up in this particular agreement. There was no power that was transferred to the federal Government from the provinces and there was no exchange of powers between the provinces.
In order to get an equal elected Senate, some of the provinces will have to give up something. I suggest to the Member that it is the height of irresponsibility to put a formula in our Constitution that will require unanimous agreement. Perhaps it could be nine out of ten provinces so that we can ensure that at least the country will proceed even if one province objects.
I respect the Hon. Member's opinion, but I think he is living in a dream world to suggest that we need the agreement of all 10 provinces when there will have to be give and take between the provinces.

Mr. Speaker, the Member makes some rather strong assertions. He accuses me of ignoring 50 years of Canadian history. My response to him is that he is ignoring immediate history.
It was thought that it was impossible to bring about a Meech Lake Accord because we could not get the unanimous consent of the provinces on such a fundamental issue. The fact is that we have managed, through the work of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and his efforts with the First Ministers, to bring about unanimous agreement. I think that speaks very well of the constitutional future of Canada.
We are in a new atmosphere which is not based on confrontation, as was the case under former Prime Minister Trudeau when, rather than compromise, negotiations and discussions with the provinces, there was confrontation and the heavy hand of the federal Government. No one felt it more than those who live in Alberta and the rest of western Canada. I believe the Meech Lake Accord is the very demonstration of the kind of attitude that can and should exist in a mature nation.
I believe this Accord speaks to the great steps Canada has made in the last few months toward maturity of a people who are united by a common vision and goal.
I know the Hon. Member's position on this issue. I think the unravelling of the Meech Lake Accord will be more destructive to Canada as we see it now and in the future than almost any other issue that exists for parliamentarians today.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in this very important debate on proposed changes to the Canadian Constitution, and to speak in support of New Democratic Party amendments which will be proposed to provide fairness to northern Canadians, open up the constitutional process for Canada's aboriginal peoples, and provide constitutional assurance that sexual equality will be protected under the new Accord.
It is easy to find a number of flaws in the Accord, but we do not want to do that. We believe that this Accord represents a very important step in Canadian constitutional history, so we have not been so much interested in looking at flaws as in looking at the important things that the Constitution does.
At the same time, the three areas I just mentioned are ones where we believe the Government can make changes without jeopardizing the Accord. We urge the Government to consider them, and we enter into this debate in good faith trusting that the Government will do so, in spite of some of the statements it has made in the past.
The Meech Lake Accord tackles the unfinished work from 1982 when we patriated the Canadian Constitution. Two major problems remained unsolved: first, bringing Quebec fully into the Constitution; second, adequately defining the rights of aboriginal people.
October 1, 1987

The question that we face today is how we say yes to Quebec without saying no to aboriginal people. I want to look at both of these issues separately.
First, let us consider the question of Quebec. It has been pointed out that legally, Quebec has been a member of the Canadian federation all along and that the 1982 Constitution included Quebec whether or not it signed. However, the report draws a distinction between legality and legitimacy.
Perhaps it is best stated by Mr. Yves Fortier, former President of the Canadian Bar Association, who said:
From a strictly legal point of view, of course, the 1982 Constitution Act applies to Quebec. But in this area, as in many others, lawyers must show some modesty. The fact is that politically, and even morally, the 1982 Constitution Act does not apply to Quebec. Those who claim it does are guilty of constitutional heresy.
With the patriation process, many people within Quebec felt that the promises of a renewed federalism that had been made at the time of the referendum debate in Quebec had been betrayed. Perhaps no one stated that more eloquently than Solange Chaput-Rolland who testified before the committee. I want to read at length from her testimony. She said:
I think none outside Quebec knew the reality of the referendum. I travelled throughout Canada, about a few months after. It was all over, eh? Good. It was not exactly all over. Families against families, towns against towns, father and mothers not speaking to their children.
(During the Referendum) we spoke with thousands of Quebeckers. Women wanted to leave their children a country as big as the one they had received from their father. That was mainly the article that reached the heart, because you are right: in this country if we put a little more heart into what we are doing, maybe we would be aware of the hurt we inflict on others.
And then we came home. We went back to the National Assembly, back to our villages, back to our houses, back to the friends that were no more friends; they were on the "yes", we were on the "no". It was not a picnic, it was not a social gathering, it was not a think-tank. It was a battle between brothers, a dangerous divisive battle, and we still feel it. It was not 100 years ago, it was seven years ago that we lived that referendum.
English Canada could not care less one month after, and it stung me and it stung all of us who fought so hard to remain in Canada and to Find ourselves outside of Canada.
You know, it was a very dramatic gesture when Mr. Levesque put the flag of Quebec at half mast on the day you were all celebrating here. But our hearts were at half mast too that day, because we were out of a country we had chosen to remain.
It was that sense of betrayal that has kept Quebec out of the Constitution from that time until this. All the time that Rene Levesque was the Premier of Quebec, it was impossible to make any progress. When Robert Bourassa became Premier, he put out the five points he said were necessary as conditions for Quebec to come into Confederation; first, recognition of Quebec as a distinct society, second, a greater provincial role in immigration, third, a provincial role in appointments to the Supreme Court of Canada, fourth, limitations on the federal spending power and, fifth, a veto for Quebec on constitutional amendments.
Constitution Amendment, 1987
These conditions were agreed to as agenda items by the Premiers at Edmonton in August of 1986. They formed the basis for the Meech Lake Accord. The demands of Quebec were well known and they formed the basis for debate by a number of organizations, including the New Democratic Party when it met at its convention in Montreal in March of this year.
Again, it is hard for Canadians from other parts of Canada to understand the joy that was felt by most of the people of Quebec when the Premier signed the Meech Lake Accord. I can remember the sense of elation that Members of Parliament from Quebec tried to share with the rest of us, both publicly and privately, on the day that Accord was signed. "Now I am a Canadian again", I remember one of them saying to me.
In 1945 when Hugh MacLellan wrote his classic novel about Quebec, he called it Two Solitudes. Since that time the phrase has become somewhat of a cliche when talking about Canadi-an-Quebec relations or relations within Quebec. MacLellan took his title from the words of Rilke who said:
"Love consists in this, that two solitudes protect
and touch and greet each other".
With Meech Lake it seems as though Quebec and the rest of Canada can protect and touch and greet each other in a new way. All Canadians should be able to rejoice in that fact.
Perhaps the most important idea in Rilke's statement is that the two solitudes would remain solitudes, the one would not seek to absorb or assimilate the other. Two solitudes protect and touch and greet each other, and is that not what we are attempting to do when we enshrine in our Constitution "the recognition that Quebec constitutes within Canada a distinct society"?
As so many witnesses testified before the joint committee, this is not creating a new situation but only recognizing a historical and sociological fact.
If MacLellan's Two Solitudes is an Anglophone account of English and French in Quebec, perhaps it should be looked at next to Felix-Antoine Savard's Menaud: Maitre-draveur which looks at the relationship from a strong Quebec nationalist perspective. Both novels are set in the context of a Quebec where English-speaking capital has moved in to exploit Quebec's resources and its people. Savard's novel begins with Menaud hearing and meditating on the words from Hemon's Maria Chapdelaine:

. . . Maria Chapdelaine:
Nous sommes venus il y a trois cents ans et nous sommes restes ...
Nous avions apporte d'outre-mer nos prieres et nos chansons; elles sont toujours les memes.

October 1, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
Nous avions apporte dans nos poitrines le coeur des hommes de notre pays, vaillant et vif, aussi prompt a la pitie qu'au rire, le coeur le plus humain de tous les coeurs humains:
il n'a pas change.
Nous avons marque un plan du continent nouveau, de Gaspe a Montreal, de Saint-Jean-d'Iverville a 1'Ungava, en disant:
Ici toutes les choses que nous avons apportees avec nous, notre culte, notre langue, nos vertus et jusqu'a nos faiblesses deviennent de choses sacrees, intangibles et qui devront demeurer jusqu'a la fin.

Of course, some things have changed, but at the heart of Quebec is a people who know themselves to be distinct and, together with the English speaking minority in Quebec, they constitute a distinct society.
In the referendum of 1980, the majority indicated they wanted to remain within Canada but as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) pointed out, the balance in favour of Canada was only achieved after the then Prime Minister, Pierre Elliott Trudeau, had promised a renewed federalism. A very high percentage, particularly of young francophones, voted for some form of sovereignty association. So we ignored the legitimate demands of the people and Government of Quebec at our country's peril.
Indeed, as the Lion. Member for New Westminster- Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett) pointed out to former Prime Minister Trudeau, this recognition of Quebec as a distinct society is not a sop the rest of Canada is giving to make Quebec feel good, it is something we have always known, a fact in which we have always taken pride.
It was something important to me when I was growing up in western Canada, even when I did not understand it, and, of course, I do not pretend to understand all of its ramifications even today. But Quebec is a distinct society, is an essential part of what makes Canada Canada, and not part of the United States. Rilke says "love consists in this, that two solitudes protect and touch and greet each other".
As Zebedee Nungak, co-chairman of the Inuit Committee on National Issues told the committee, there is a third solitude in Canada, the aboriginal solitude, and aboriginal peoples feel more isolated than ever before by the Meech Lake Accord. They do not feel protected. They do not feel touched by it nor do they feel greeted by it. They feel isolated. Zebedee Nungak said:
We know what it is to be on the outside looking in, so Quebec being made part of the Constitutional fabric of Canada was to us a necessity that was better dealt with sooner than later. However, in saying that, we object quite strongly to what we see as being shut out of any future process in constitutional discussions.
In their struggle to achieve even the most basic recognition in the Canadian Constitution, aboriginal people faced a very difficult time in 1980 and 1981 when we were patriating the Constitution. They appeared before the committee and made their case, pointing to the nature of their treaties, or pointing to unextinguished aboriginal rights in the case of those who had no treaties. They had support from church and solidarity
groups. I remember the many questions that we as New Democrats asked the then Prime Minister, Mr. Trudeau, and the difficult bargaining the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) went through to get aboriginal rights included in the Constitution.
I still remember the day, January 30, 1981, when the big breakthrough was made and Jean Chretien, the Minister in charge at the time, said: "Lets do it". So wording was put in recognizing aboriginal and treaty rights and defining the aboriginal peoples as Indians, Metis and Inuit.
Even then an amending formula was proposed that would have meant that Parliament could have unilaterally changed those rights for aboriginal peoples living in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, or that Parliament and the legislature of one province could affect the rights of aboriginal people in that province.
Then, on November 5, 1981, the nine provinces agreed on a constitutional package that left Quebec out. It also left out any reference to aboriginal rights or to the rights of women. Only after weeks of bitter struggle were sexual equality rights put back in, along with a very much weaker version of aboriginal rights. Aboriginal people were told not to worry about this weaker wording because they had the guarantee of a First Ministers' conference in which they would be invited to further define those rights.
A conference was held in 1983. But all that came out of it was a decision to hold three more conferences. These were also held with a great deal of rhetoric and fanfare in 1984, 1985, and the last one just this past spring.
What have the aboriginal people got out of all this work and all these conferences? A big fat nothing. These conferences have dominated their agenda for the past five years. They have absorbed the time and effort of the aboriginal leadership. After all the conferences are over, what do they have to show for them? Nothing, Mr. Speaker.
Poverty and powerlessness continue to characterize the lives of most aboriginal people. In all but one case land claims settlements have been stalled. As more aboriginal young people see the value of education and want to move on to university and college, the Government has capped the amount of money that is available for higher education. Only the prisons seem to be able to expand to meet the challenge.
Can we blame aboriginal people if they become bitter after all this struggle when they see the First Ministers reach a quick settlement with Quebec? They feel that the provinces lack the political will to deal with aboriginal rights. They feel that the Prime Minister has not given the kind of leadership and commitment to their cause that he did to getting Quebec back into the Constitution.
The aboriginal people are very worried that this new Accord promises further constitutional conferences on such items as
October 1, 1987

fisheries, which are absolutely essential to aboriginal people, but the aboriginal people and their leaders will not have a place at the table when fisheries are being dicussed. So they feel that this Accord leaves them further behind than ever.
The Special Joint Committee suggests that they do not need to worry about this. If I have one complaint with the report, and I have a few, this is perhaps the major one. It says that the joint committee takes the view that for these purposes aboriginal people, like other Canadians, are appropriately represented by the leaders of the federal and provincial Governments that aboriginal peoples helped to elect.
Aboriginal people have seen how their interests have been sold out. They were sold out on November 5, 1981, by the provinces and the federal Government when they wanted to cobble together a deal. They know how easy it is for their issues to be pushed to one side. This statement in this report is not something that aboriginal peoples can put any credence in whatsoever. How can we expect them to have any confidence in the federal and provincial Governments when they remember such days as November 5 when they were pushed aside? When push comes to shove in the fisheries, do any of us seriously believe that this Government will stand up for aboriginal rights if it were to jeopardize its relationships with the provinces?
The Prime Minister has continued to use rhetoric about his support for aboriginal self-government. But, last week when he was asked, he would not give a commitment to place aboriginal self-government on the agenda at this specific time. He would not give a commitment to restore constitutional funding so that aboriginal organizations could do the necessary preparation. This is in spite of the kind of recommendations that the committee made.
I would just like to read some of these items from the conclusion of the report. It affirmed the view that the First Ministers and representatives of aboriginal people must continue to work toward a satisfactory resolution of the constitutional issues brought forward by the aboriginal peoples, especially the issue of aboriginal self-government. It recommends that the federal Government restore funding to aboriginal organizations at an appropriate level to enable them to continue to participate in the preparatory work. It recommends that a timetable and serious work plan be established by the federal Government in consultation with the provinces and the aboriginal organizations to prepare for a further constitutional conference or conferences on aboriginal self-government. It recommends that consideration be given to holding these conferences in closed sessions, and that the first such conference take place no later than April 17, 1990.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I welcome this Accord insofar as it enables Quebec to come back into Confederation, not only as a full partner but also with recognition of its distinct character. But I urge the Government to accept New Democratic Party amendments that would not damage the Accord but would prevent the Accord from doing an injustice to
Constitution Amendment, 1987
aboriginal people, prevent it from doing an injustice to the people of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories and that would assure the women of Canada that their rights are protected.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Are there questions or comments?

I would like to compliment the Hon. Member on his contribution to this debate, although I take issue with his way of describing the reality of the Accord and the reality of what I believe is Quebec and Canadian society today. I would like to ask him this.
He referred to the quotation from Rilke, I believe, "two solitudes which protect and greet each other". I would like to ask him: Why not promote? Of course that was not in her quotation. She did not say "promote" the linguistic minorities around the country. If we are so caring about the French fact and the English fact, and if there is such goodwill, which he seems to believe there is, why would we not out of the goodness of our hearts, then, take the step of stating in our Constitution that we are prepared not only to preserve the status quo, to preserve the linguistic minorities wherever they may be in the country, but that we would be willing to promote these minorities? Is that not a very clear indication that the language of the Accord does not indicate the kind of goodwill which he seems to believe prevails?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question. As I indicated, I think it is easy enough to see areas in which this Accord could be improved. Personally, I have no objection to seeing the word "promote" included. I think that might be a helpful inclusion.
What I am saying is that it is important for Canada at this particular stage of our history to say yes to Quebec. I weigh a number of factors about the Accord which I do not particularly care for, but I place those in the balance. I also place the question of saying yes to Quebec in the balance, and that weighs very heavily.
I also want to remind the Government that these other three issues which we have raised of justice to Canada's northern citizens, opening the door to constitutional participation by the aboriginal peoples of Canada, and giving an assurance to Canadian women that the Accord will not affect sexual equality in Canada, are weighing very heavily in the balance, not only for Members of Parliament but for the Canadian people. I urge the Government to take those issues very seriously.

Again, I wish to return to my question to the Hon. Member. He states that this agreement meets with the approval of the Government of Quebec. That is true. I would suggest to him that the Government of Quebec has the responsibility for its own prerogatives and concerns for the territory of the Province of Quebec, but I would suggest that the Hon. Member and his Party, and the Members of the House, have a responsibility to the entire country.

October 1, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
The Province of Quebec may feel that it is satisfactory to state that we will recognize the existence of minorities, which in a grudging fashion are described as being present but not necessarily a whole or integral part of Quebec society. It may very well suit the Governments of Alberta and Manitoba to say that minorities are only present in that part of the country, but again we have a responsibility for the national perspective.
The head of the Federation des Francophones Hors Quebec appeared before the constitutional committee and certainly was not happy with the status quo. Only last week the head of the Franco-Albertan Association stated that to them the Meech Lake Agreement meant assimilation. Is the Hon. Member happy to support an agreement which will probably mean the assimilation of the French minority outside Quebec, and God only knows what it means for the English minority in Quebec.

I have heard Members in the House who belong to francophone minorities outside Quebec state that they are concerned about the continuation of their language outside Quebec, and indicate to the House that they did not feel that this Accord threatened the continuation of the French language outside Quebec. I believe that they are much closer to the situation than I am, and even closer to the situation than the Hon. Member. On that basis, I am prepared to accept their assurance that the Accord does not threaten the continuation.
I note that the colleague of the Hon. Member, the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de Grace-Lachine East who is an Anglophone from within Quebec, will support the Accord. 1 have some trust in his concern for the anglophone minority in Quebec, and some of the concerns raised by other Members from Quebec, even though the Hon. Member disagrees with his colleagues from Quebec.
In conclusion, I do not claim that I am an expert on the question of language within Quebec, or the rights of francophones outside Quebec. But at this time I am prepared to take the assurance of Members who represent those groups that they are protected, even though I recognize within the anglophone minority in Quebec there is some division on this question.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Hon. Member who is not from Quebec whether he made his decision to support the Meech Lake Accord as a Canadian Member of this House, as a Member of the Parliament of Canada, to ensure that all the component parts of Canada are indeed a part of Canada? This is not strictly a Quebec decision. I think the decision is one to be made by all Canadian Members of Parliament who must ensure that Quebec is part of Confederation.
My next question is as follows. In 1982 we had an imperfect accord. If I remember correctly, the Hon. Member supported the 1982 Accord. He knew perfectly well that Quebec was not in Confederation, and despite warnings by prophets of doom
and gloom, similar to what we have heard today, Quebec has now become a member of Confederation. Is the Honourable Member-I want to congratulate him on his decision- confident that the next generation, tomorrow's generation, will be as generous in dealing with the proposals and groups that have been left out as the people who were left out in 1982?

Certainly, if I was going to look at the Accord from the narrow point of view of a British Columbian, I would have a lot of trouble with it. For one thing, it does not deal with the Senate which, as a British Columbian, I feel very strongly about. With a population of 2.8 million, British Columbia has six members in the Senate, whereas Provinces such as Nova Scotia or New Brunswick have 10 Members in the Senate, so there is a great imbalance. If I was looking at this issue strictly from a parochial point of view, I would have a lot of difficulty with the Accord. I am not denying that I have some difficulty with it even so.
The question of including Quebec is absolutely crucial. Equally crucial is the question of providing justice to aboriginal people. The aboriginal people were the original inhabitants of Canada, and for us to ignore them and to continue ignoring them in our Constitution, is unconscionable. It is on that basis that I voted against the 1982 Constitution on the basis that it did not give adequate recognition to the rights of Canada's aboriginal peoples.
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, many of us are in a catch-22 situation with respect to this important constitutional resolution.
In 1980 we in the Liberal Party fought hard and in great numbers against the sovereignty association proposal at the time of the Quebec referendum. That was a pseudo-separatist proposal that was put before us in Quebec. We fought hard and won; a majority of francophone Quebecers voted against that proposal, and a majority of anglophone Quebecers voted against that proposal.
At the time of the referendum, the people of Quebec stated that they wanted to be fully part of Canada, and they rejected any type of quasi-separation. Unfortunately, in the constitutional talks that followed in 1981 and 1982 when we patriated the Constitution and added an amending formula and a Charter of Rights, the Quebec Government of the day, which was the Parti Quebecois separatist Government, did not agree to it. They voted against it. We may have expected them to do that because we know that the Parti Quebecois had no great interest in the unity of Canada, in a new Constitution, or in an amending formula. We expected that from them, but I should remind the House that the Liberal Party in Quebec, which is a moderate federalist Party, also voted with the Parti Quebecois in the National Assembly against the Constitutional Accord of 1982.
October 1, 1987

Since that time, Quebec has not been a full participant in constitutional discussions in Canada. Many of us regret that. We want Quebec fully participating in the Canadian constitutional process. We need Quebec, we love Quebec, and we want them with us 100 per cent.
In 1985 with the election of the Bourassa Liberals, this federalist Party made a new attempt to adhere to the Constitution of 1982, and to the full constitutional process.
Mr. Bourassa laid down five proposals for adherence to the Constitution: Quebec should be recognized as a distinct society; Quebec should have increased power in immigration; there should be a limitation of the federal spending power in areas of provincial jurisdiction; there should be a revision of the amending formula to recognize Quebec's long standing veto power; Quebec should be allowed to participate in the appointment of judges to the Supreme Court of Canada. Those were the five conditions or proposals that the Quebec Government laid down for rejoining the constitutional family in Canada. The federal Liberal Party was the first to respond in a positive manner to those five proposals.
In the summer of 1986, in an interview in Le Devoir, our Leader responded in a positive way to the five proposals. In November, 1986, the Liberal Party of Canada, at its national convention, passed a resolution which responded in a positive way to the five proposals. A little later the NDP passed similar resolutions which responded in a positive way to them.
Finally, on May 1, 1987, all the provinces and the federal Government agreed unanimously to the Meech Lake Accord which contained the five proposals. It was an historic moment, a moment of great national reconciliation. What was interesting was that we had nine provinces with a majority of anglophones saying "yes" to Quebec after Quebec had said "yes" to Canada in the 1980 referendum.
Among those nine provinces we had three with Liberal Governments, one with an NDP Government, one with a Social Credit Government, and five with Conservative Governments. Some of those provinces were rich. Some were poor. Some were large. Some were small. It was amazing that the 10 provinces and the federal Government should respond in a positive way to the overtures which Quebec had been making.
However, it was unfortunate in a way that not only did the Meech Lake Accord and the follow-up Langevin agreement respond to the five proposals laid down by Mr. Bourassa, but they went beyond that. They included other matters which were not originally raised by Mr. Bourassa. In addition, there were certain ambiguities and unclear parts. It was not sure whether or not, in agreeing to what Mr. Bourassa had requested, we were touching in a negative way on the rights of others in the Constitution.
Constitution Amendment, 1987
As I said at the beginning of my remarks, some of us are in a bit of a dilemma. We want to say "yes" to Quebec. We want to say "yes" to this agreement. We think it is extremely important to do so. However, we do not want to do anything which would diminish already existing rights in the Constitution or to block the development of other rights in the Constitution. It is a bit of a dilemma.
We in the Liberal Party say-and the joint committee on the Constitution said it as well-that there are certain flaws in the agreement. Everybody recognizes that. However, the joint committee, having recognized that there were certain flaws, said that we should not try to amend it, that we should pass it as it is, and that in the next round we should try to correct the flaws. We say that that is not the way to go. There are certain flaws which can be corrected without denying, in any way, the five conditions laid down by Mr. Bourassa. We are not suggesting for a moment that we should introduce or pass any amendment which would fly in the face of the five original proposals of Mr. Bourassa.
We have formulated nine amendments to correct serious flaws which we think need to be corrected. We do not believe that correcting any one of the flaws by way of any one of our nine amendments will in any way take away from the five conditions of Mr. Bourassa.
One amendment is already before the House. It concerns the fact that the aboriginal peoples of Canada make up part of the fundamental characteristic of Canada and that the multicultural heritage and make-up of Canada must be considered. It is a misconception to think that the fundamental characteristic of Canada is simply a question of anglophone and francophone. That may have been the case in 1867, but if we look at Canada today, we see that it consists of anglophones, francophones, aboriginals, and a large number of people who have come from many other countries and cultures. In our amendment we wanted the interpretive clause which defines the fundamental characteristic of Canada reworded in that way.
Another amendment would have the federal Government and the provinces not only preserving minority language groups but also promoting minority language groups, such as francophones outside Quebec and anglophones in Quebec.
In a third amendment we want to extend the non-derogation provisions of Section 16 to the whole Charter, not simply to the questions of aboriginal rights and multicultural rights.
We have also proposed in a further amendment that when there are vacancies in the Senate they should be filled by an election in the province where the vacancy occurs, not by an appointment by the provincial Premier. We think that is a good interim measure on the way to a fully elected Senate.
In a further proposal we are suggesting that the territories should have a say in the nomination of candidates for judgeships to the Supreme Court of Canada. I do not know whether when the provinces sat down with the federal Government to

Some people feel this part could be used to remove existing language rights. It has been suggested in my own province that in some way or other, by recognizing the distinctiveness of Quebec society and giving the Government the right to promote that distinctiveness, it could remove the rights of the Anglophone minority. I see nothing in the Accord that will do that. To the contrary. If you read the document, it very clearly states:
-and English-speaking Canadians, concentrated outside Quebec but also
present in Quebec, constitutes a fundamental characteristic of Canada-
It goes on to say:
(2)	The role of the Parliament of Canada and the provincial legislatures to preserve the fundamental characteristic of Canada referred to in paragraph (l)(a) is affirmed.
In other words, in signing this document Quebec pledged itself to preserve the English-speaking fact in Quebec, and there is nothing in the document anywhere which takes away any of the other entrenched rights which are found in our constitutional documents, Section 133 of the BNA in 1867, or Section 23 of the Constitution Act, 1982. Nothing. I challenge those people who say there is a derogation of anglophone rights in Quebec to show me the clauses that will do that.
What they are doing in many cases is drawing a scenario and exaggerating it in the extreme. It is mainly speculation. We have had attacks on anglophone rights in Quebec for a long time, especially under the Parti Quebecois. There was no Meech Lake Accord then. Whether we have one or not, there will be individuals and political Parties in Quebec who want to attack minority rights. I agree with this Accord but I must remind Mr. Bourassa that he made a promise to anglophones in Quebec to amend the sign legislation to bring about justice with respect to bilingual signs. We expect him to deliver on that promise.
As I say, there is nothing in this Accord that will derogate from the rights of minorities in Canada. To the contrary, I think there is a small but meaningful contribution to the entrenchment of minority language rights. My colleague from Saint Henri-Westmount was in the Cabinet in 1982. So was my colleague from Davenport. My colleague sitting behind me from Laurier was in the caucus. It was at that time I voted against that document because there was a reduction of anglophone rights in Quebec. I must remind Canadians of that fact. I voted against that document because there was a very specific reduction in Section 59, and my colleagues agreed to it. I do not know where the great spirit they have shown today in defending minority rights was at that time. They were in the Cabinet but they did not resign in protest, that is for sure.
You are giving me the sign that my time is up, Mr. Speaker. Yet there is so much in the document to discuss. Let me say that if anyone can point out to me one clause in this document that leads to the reduction of minority language rights, I will vote against it. I challenge them to show me one clause that does that. They cannot.
Constitution Amendment, 1987
On balance, despite its flaws which I would like the Government to correct by accepting some of these amendments, it is an historic document of reconciliation. After nine provinces have said yes to Quebec, it is very difficult for us in this House to say no to the reconciliation which brings all Canadians and all provinces together.

speechtext: Questions and comments.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to humbly try and respond to the Hon. Member's challenge. He is very well aware of the distinct society provision in the clause and I suggest that if any clause could affect the rights of Quebecers and minorities in Quebec, it certainly would be that clause. I suppose by his reasoning he believes that clause has no legal significance. Is that his conclusion, that it means nothing? I suppose if that is the case, we are talking about nothing. Yet it clearly has to mean something, or it must mean nothing. I put it to him that it does mean something.
He is a lawyer. I also had a bit of legal training. I think one of the first things we learn in law school is that the-

The legislator never speaks to say nothing.
Therefore, I would suggest to him that the clause must have some significance. I would refer him to the comments of the Premier of Quebec, Mr. Bourassa.
[ Translation]
-who had this to say to the National Assembly last June 18: "Henceforth the Constitution of the country will have to be interpreted in accordance with this recognition". He was referring to the recognition of Quebec as a distinct society. He said, and I quote: "It must be emphasized that the whole Constitution, including the Charter, will be interpreted and applied in light of this distinct society section. This relates to the exercise of legislative powers and will enable us to consolidate acquired rights and make progress."
So I respectfully suggest to the Hon. Member that Mr. Bourassa should know what he is talking about, and that the words of this provision should normally mean something.
Does he believe that Mr. Bourassa is right or wrong, and that in the end this does not mean anything?

Mr. Speaker, I never suggested for one minute that this clause means nothing. The Hon. Member should not put words in my mouth. Of course it means something. It is an interpretive clause. It starts off by saying that the Constitution of Canada shall be interpreted in a manner consistent with the fundamental characteristic of Canada and the recognition that Quebec constitutes within Canada a distinct society.

October 1, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
Of course the clause means something. It is similar to Section 27 of the Constitutional Act of 1982 which says that the Charter shall be interpreted in a manner consistent with the preservation and enhancement of the multicultural heritage of Canadians. The opening words of the distinct society clause are almost exactly the same as those of Section 27.
What does it mean to recognize Quebec as a distinct society within Canada and that Quebec has the right to promote that? I think it means exactly what the Quebec Court of Appeal ruled in the signs case. In the signs case, the Quebec Court of Appeal, in a unanimous decision, ruled that Bill 101 was unconstitutional when it said other languages could not be used on signs. It ruled that it was unconstitutional to forbid other languages but it said that if Quebec wanted to pass a law requiring the use of French on signs, that was its right.
What was proposed by Mr. Bourassa in the election was a new option whereby Quebec would require French on all commercial signs but not forbid the use of any other language, whether it be English, Polish, Chinese, Italian or whatever. There they are promoting the distinct society but not taking away rights from others, because in my opinion, they cannot do that.
The previous clause says there is an English fact in Quebec and it says it is the role of the Government of Canada, the Parliament of Canada and the provincial Legislatures to preserve that fundamental characteristic. Quebec has committed itself to preserving the anglophone minority in Quebec, not just in 133 or in Section 23 but also by virtue of the Meech Accord.
Sure the clause means something. When I promote my own distinctiveness, my own career or my own family, I do not need to do it at the expense of others. I do it to further my own causes. I think that is what that clause is saying. Unfortunately, some people in Quebec and across Canada think that in order to promote one's own causes, one must take away from others. That is not the case.
I can build and improve my own home without stealing lumber and bricks from my neighbour next door. I can make it the best home on the block, but I do not have to detract from anybody else. Promoting one's distinctiveness does not take anything away from anybody else, including the minorities in Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the comments of my colleague across the floor. I think I personally as an Ontario anglophone have a better understanding of what the distinct society means to a person who lives in Quebec, such as the Hon. Member.
Going back into history and bringing us up to date, it would seem Quebec has always been a distinct society, but that has only been recognized at this particular time. The Hon.
Member did not discuss, though I know he has some familiarity with it, immigration and how it affects Quebec. My understanding is that Quebec has always had a say in immigration. There will be some changes under the Accord regarding immigration. Does he have any trouble with that particular clause?

Mr. Speaker, as Hon. Members know, the responsibility for immigration under our Constitution has been a joint federal-provincial responsibility since 1867, although the provinces did not exercise any legislative power under that right for many, many years. I think Quebec was probably the first province to want to exercise that power.
It is a joint power. Unlike some other powers, it gives both the provinces and the federal Government the right to pass legislation with respect to immigration. However, it also says that the federal power will prevail over the provincial power. By the way, so does this document.
Clause 3(2) says about immigration that an agreement that has the force of law under this subsection shall have effect only so long and so far as it is not repugnant to any provision of an Act of the Parliament of Canada that sets national standards and objectives. The Province of Quebec and other provinces can pass legislation in the area of immigration as long as it is not repugnant to the federal legislation. It has been that way in more general terms since 1867 but never spelled out this way.
When the Liberals were in power, we made an agreement with Quebec which has been followed since that time, and it has not caused any great harm. As a matter of fact, I think it has helped Quebec and Canada in selecting immigrants for that province. To put it in the Constitution would not cause any great harm. Not only would it not cause any great harm, if it settles old wars, all the better.

First, Mr. Speaker, I should like to commend the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) for his remarks. From a legal standpoint I think he showed clearly that the question of distinct character in facts has always existed, but that at last Canada agrees to put that in the Constitution and protect the future.
Those who are opposed to the distinct character provision of the Meech Lake Accord accuse others who endorse it to be provincially oriented Members, narrow-minded people who stand up only for the interests of Quebec. The Hon. Member has been in this House for a good many years-and I share all his views concerning the amendments, I can blame the federal Government and all provincial administrations for failing to add other things-he is not afraid to stand up and, as an anglophone, he agrees with the distinct character provision. That being the case, does he feel like a provincially oriented Member here in the House of Commons, or does he feel he is on the same wavelength as all other Members because he
October 1, 1987

agrees with that, because he is a Member who stands up for the rights of all Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, I defend that provision because I think it serves the unity of all Canada. It is good for all of Canada. As I said, Quebec said yes to Canada in the referendum of 1980, but we had to wait until this Accord with the nine other provinces of many political backgrounds and the federal Government saying yes to Quebec. To me, that was a great act of national reconciliation because we need and want Quebec at the constitutional table. Something was missing without Quebec, and it is fantastic to have it back.
I think it is for the good of all the country. When I support this, it is not because I am from Quebec or because I am a provincialist. If the Hon. Member supports it or somebody on the other side supports it, I think it is because they are very concerned with the unity of Canada and the epanouissement of Canada. It is for the good of all of Canada that this be done.

1.	The Constitution Act, 1867 is amended by adding thereto, immediately after section 1 thereof, the following section:
"2. (1) The Constitution of Canada shall be interpreted in a manner consistent with
(a)	the recognition that the existence of French-speaking Canadians, centred in Quebec but also present elsewhere in Canada, and Englishspeaking Canadians, concentrated outside Quebec but also present in Quebec, constitutes a fundamental characteristic of Canada; and
(b)	the recognition that Quebec constitutes within Canada a distinct society.
(2)	The role of the Parliament of Canada and the provincial legislatures to preserve the fundamental characteristic of Canada referred to in paragraph (l)(a) is affirmed.
(3)	The role of the legislature and Government of Quebec to preserve and promote the distinct identity of Quebec referred to in paragraph (l)(b) is affirmed.
(4)	Nothing in this section derogates from the powers, rights or privileges of Parliament or the Government of Canada, or of the legislatures or governments of the provinces, including any powers, rights or privileges relating to language."

(2) Until an amendment to the Constitution of Canada is made in relation to the Senate pursuant to section 41 of the Constitution Act, 1982, the person summoned to fill a vacancy in the Senate shall be chosen from among persons whose names have been submitted under subsection (1) by the government of the province to which the vacancy relates and must be acceptable to the Queen's Privy Council for Canada."

Mr. Speaker, I am particularly happy to take part in this debate today, not because of the simple fact that I am a native and come from one of the Territories but because I was elected largely on a constitutional platform.
In my area, the Inuit homeland of the Northwest Territories which we call Nunavut for the time being, constitutional rights such as land claims, regional councils, regional boards of all kinds, et cetera, et cetera, dominate our discussions. Our people have always searched for a way in which our territory can become part of Canada and enjoy the full rights of the Constitution.
I wish to make it very clear that while we are seeking our own constitutional goals we do not deny others their rights. The Meech Lake Accord was a remarkable achievement by governments among which any agreement is usually remarkable. It provides protections which have enabled the population of Quebec to re-enter the national life. I can only applaud that and I can only hope that all northerners will also applaud that.
We are in a very dangerous situation in Canada if the victory of one group becomes the envy and resentment of others. Sharing is perhaps the most sacred value in Inuit society. Our people wish to achieve certain things and that does not mean we begrudge the good fortune of others. On the other hand, the achievement of this Meech Lake agreement shows the way. It provides a demonstration of how agreements can be reached when there is political will. In the North we need a lot of political will now. Part of that agreement is to hold further conferences, which I support.
In those fora we cannot doubt that items of concern to northerners will be discussed. I have no fears about us being left out as some people in the North have been saying recently.
The report of the special joint committee makes some specific recommendations. On aboriginal rights the report recommends a process and funds for work which I support. The following chapter on the impact of Meech Lake on the northern Territories highlights the question which must concern us all-how the aboriginal homelands of northern Canada and the Metis, Indian and Inuit people who live in them can be reconciled with provincial-type structures. I will have more to say about that, too.

October 1, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
The Meech Lake Accord is a piece of nation building. There are other pieces of our nation which must be completed. In the Northwest Territories and the Yukon we have 40 per cent of the land area of Canada but not the political and economic rights taken for granted in the south. For example, northerners have no control over their lands and resources. Northerners have no control over what goes on in our inland seas even though Canada's Inuit provide the national argument our lawyers take to world bodies to claim those ocean waters.
Inuit use of the seas and sea ice are the basis of that claim. I noticed that before the Venice Economic Summit President Reagan spoke of our unique Inuit claim. He said that he thought it could provide a basis for agreement between Canada and the United States about those waters.
Of course the North is larger than just the Territories. Northern Quebec and Labrador have vast Arctic areas inhabited by Inuit. Five other provinces also have large subArctic areas. Outside of a few boom-towns like Tuktoyaktuk on the Beaufort Sea or Iqaluit on South Baffin Island, the permanent residents are aboriginal in nature.
There are two approaches to constitutional development in the North today. Members of this House have heard submissions by Governments of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon which, by the way, I sympathize with. The problem, as they see it, is a conventional one. For example, by being promised provincehood in the future they say they can deal with the social and political problems. As a Member representing a predominantly native riding, specifically an Inuit riding, this is where I part company with the political views of my fellow territorial residents in the Mackenzie area. That is, of course, with all due respect to the views of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson). As a result, I have been accused of not supporting the position of the Territories by both the Government of the Northwest Territories and by the media in the North.
The Inuit approach to our social and political problems has always been a complete overhaul of the political system in the North. Specifically, one has been the settlement of aboriginal claims to the land and resources and the right to govern ourselves by the modification of a territorial form of government, the creation of a Nunavut territory out of the existing one. Unfortunately, this view is opposed by our present colonial masters, the settlers of Canada residing in the Northwest Territories.
Consequently, and in view of the situation in the North, I can only envy the two so-called founding nations-the English and francophone nations, who have resolved their co-existence through the Meech Lake Accord. As a result I will support this Accord because it paves the way for other peoples of Canada with different political and social goals to one day resolve their own differences.
I do not know a great deal of constitutional law, but I was working on constitutional matters for many years before my election. Constitutions are social documents written in legal
fora by lawyers. However, first, a constitution must express a social truth.
I headed the Nunavut land claims project at one time. For those people who do not yet understand, land claims is really the aboriginal peoples' constitutional approach. Our people know that the land and waters which provide our life are the basis of everything so it is natural for us to identify ourselves with them. We build our ideas of society up from there. We have ways of life carefully suited to the land we live in. That land, the Arctic, is a very special place. I am glad that many southern people have the chance, through television and photography books, to learn about it now. However, ultimately, we Inuit believe that we have a special responsibility for our land. We wish to exercise that responsibility through management systems and self-government.
Therefore, we continue to negotiate land claims and at the same time we work to create a Nunavut government. Ottawa, in its wisdom, long ago decided that these two processes must be separate, although to Inuit they are one. Therefore, we have two sets of offices and two sets of staff, but they work closely together. Sometimes we think that the southern negotiators like the two processes so that they can play one off against the other. However, we Inuit are very clear about what we want.
If I have a criticism of the Special Joint Committee report it is that the northern chapter thinks strictly in terms of provincial status. It is very conventional. Gordon Robertson, among other experts on northern policy, has written a book about the fact that more flexible arrangements would be more workable. He, like we, wants arrangements which do not force Inuit into a southern mould. Nunavut is our answer.
1 do not understand why the special joint committee does not mention Nunavut. Perhaps they did not listen to the Inuit. Certainly they did not understand us. Indian groups also have ideas for self-government but the special joint committee has not spoken for native northerners; the Metis, Indian, and Inuit people who are the permanent residents of the North, when it discusses the future purely in terms of the provincial path.
That section is too conventional, too rigid. It totally ignores the fact, for instance, that in the Northwest Territories two constitutional fora have been working for the past five years and in fact reached an accord last winter. This northern accord has yet to be put to a referendum.
Those forums, the western constitutional forum and the Nunavut constitutional forum are bringing aboriginal and white legislative members and aboriginal association leaders to a social and political census on new governments. Nunavut is the Inuit proposal.
I must raise this subject because there is some evidence that people in Ottawa and in the south generally do not understand the issue. The modern history of the Northwest Territories is not a happy one. The feelings among the regions and peoples have not always been friendly. If federal policy ignores the
October 1, 1987

regional reality, the cultural reality, and the long stated demands of Inuit through land claims, through talks on a Nunavut Government, through the national constitutional talks, then there can be no progress. The northern chapter of the report briskly assumes northerners can be quickly marched into a southern parade. I would suggest that policy-makers not be quite so certain of that.
Just as I support the spirit of commitment and creativity which led to the Meech Lake Accord, so I look forward to another such process to deal with Inuit and other northern and aboriginal issues.
If almost half of Canada-the North-is in limbo as some people have said, that is serious. We need a more active commitment in Ottawa to assisting northern people sort out the remaining problems in creating new territorial governments. Nunavut is an opportunity for Canada. It is the best answer to anyone in the world who thinks that Canadians treat aboriginal people like South Africans treat blacks.
I want to take this opportunity to elaborate on the concerns raised by the two territorial Governments relating to provincial status. If the two Territories are so concerned about this issue of provincehood, there is a practical way to resolve it even though it would involve a major constitutional conference involving all the First Ministers of this country, with the two Territories involved this time.
Given that both the non-native and aboriginal residents are similar in political and cultural persuasion, why not merge the territory of the Yukon and the western part of Northwest Territories to make one territory and, consequently, an eleventh province? They would then have the appropriate political maturity, including the raw numbers to warrant it. We could then have only one Territory left in the Canadian Confederation, a native territory which could then become Canada's showcase to the world.
I urge all Hon. Members, as well as the First Ministers, to study this alternative as a viable way of satisfying everyone's political aspirations, including the two territorial Governments which have felt left out so far.
The reason there has been a move for the creation of two territories is that there are two almost equally divided groups of people. One group wants to work toward provincial status while the other wishes to safeguard its culture, its land and its people through the creation of their own territory. This is where I said I have parted company with the views expressed by the Government of the Northwest Territories.
The northern political constitutional question is not a provincial question. It is largely an aboriginal question. Inuit have always made clear that our proposals for Nunavut welcome the white people who live among us. We have no desire to discriminate against anyone.
While Ottawa is turning over powers and budgets to the Yellowknife Government, territorial officials, including the politicians in Yellowknife, are delighted but will not admit it.
Constitution Amendment, 1987
They believe that this will kill Nunavut, but it will not. Nunavut will not go away because it is the way we Inuit think of our land. Nunavut means "our land". We will not be happy living in a Yellowknife-dominated territory.
This summer, Nick Sibbeston, the NWT government leader, said that having more power in Yellowknife means that Nunavut is no longer needed. That could not be farther from the truth. He certainly does not understand Inuit or the eastern half of the territory over which he is territorial premier.
Inuit need a government which speaks our own language. We need a government that takes on the hard issues of resource management and development, and which helps us restore peace and stability in some of our villages which have grown too fast. That government is Nunavut.
In conclusion, we can identify with the people of Quebec to full political participation in Canada through the Meech Lake Accord. We know what it feels like to be left out. It is these problems which aboriginal and northern people bring to Ottawa in the hope of justice. I call upon the House and Canadian people to complete the infrastructure of nationhood. I call on you all to work to make the North part of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, first let me congratulate my hon. colleague from the North for stating a very important point that I believe was not made well during the discussions at Meech Lake. It concerns the diversity within Canada both of the traditional concepts of government and the aboriginal concept related to self-government, aboriginal rights and meeting the needs of those areas such as the one represented by my colleague, which is largely made up of aboriginal people. Those views are of great benefit to this discussion because I believe Canadians are not aware of them.
On the other hand, I disagree with some of the positions taken by my colleague. Originally I thought the boundary extension clause in the Constitution may have referred to the south, but then I was told that the States may not like that. I then had to assume that the boundary extension clause referred to the North, but now the Member says that it means east and west, with the Yukon becoming part of the Northwest Territories or vice versa.
It is an interesting concept and probably one of the best original thoughts we have heard in this debate. While the Member receives high points for originality, I do not believe that concept will be welcomed with great rejoicing in the Yukon.
The Hon. Member mentioned the aspirations of the Inuit. Those of us who live in the North, while not Inuit, hopefully understand some of the issues and empathize with those aspirations.
I am concerned about how the Member believes the Meech Lake Accord contributes to the advancement of Nunavut, for

October 1, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
instance. Upon review of the process to date, does the Eton. Member know ijf the Inuit were consulted before, during or after the First Ministers' conference that resulted in the Meech Lake Accord?

Mr. Speaker, to be quite frank, the short answer would probably be no, considering that the two territorial Governments Were not consulted.
On the other hand, I believe that we in the North, especially the Inuit and the Inuit Committee on National Issues, do not oppose the two major founding peoples, the francophones and anglophones, settling their differences first. Like it or not, the Inuit is a very small minority within those two systems, and to be quite frank, in order to be successful in our aspirations, we have to co-operate more with those nations than perhaps some of the other aboriginal peoples in Canada.
The short answer is that, as an aboriginal Member, I certainly was not consulted, but I think that is beside the point now. I had earlier mentioned that I was elected on the issue of resolving some major questions which affect all of us. I think the Meech Lake Agreement required something very strong, and that is the only answer I can provide at this time.

I thank the Hon. Member for that answer. I think that has clarified some of my question. I very much agree that the concept of self-government for aboriginal people is absolutely essential to the development of this country, that there needs to be a much greater understanding of that concept within our society, that it will not undermine provincial status or territorial legislatures, that it is the right thing to do and that it is something that will work. We have to deal with what is being done here. How does my colleague see the Meech Lake Accord resolutions helping to further aboriginal self-government and the creation in the Eastern Arctic of NunaVut? How does he see the Accord facilitating that? My concern is that I see it detracting from that.

Mr. Speaker, I will answer the question in two ways. First, according to the summary of the joint committee on the Senate and House of Commons, the Accord itself would require future First Ministers' conferences on constitutional change to deal with any other outstanding concerns, and I would have to rely on that. The other part of the answer would be that up until now the federal Government has allowed the NWT, in particular, to be able to resolve its political differences on its own at the very outset. We are getting very close to that.
I mentioned earlier that there is in fact a political accord which, unfortunately, has not yet been put to a plebiscite or referendum, but we expect that after next Monday's territorial elections, our representatives are going to make sure that this issue of resolving the boundary dispute will be put to a referendum. That is my second answer.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member in his comments referred to the question of provincial status. He suggested that there may be a practical way to resolve this. I think he referred to a constitutional conference in which the Governments of the Territories would participate. I would like him, though, to perhaps add a word or two about the question of unanimity. How does he feel about this particular provision of the Meech Lake Agreement that will require the unanimous agreement of the provinces, and the federal Government, in order to create new provinces?
As the Hon. Member knows, the western provinces were created by an agreement between the Governments of those provinces, the Territories that were to become provinces, and the federal Government. There is probably something to say for giving the provinces a greater say in creating new provinces because it will affect the amending formula. So the two questions are certainly linked.
However, does the Hon. Member not feel that by requiring the unanimous agreement of the provinces it is really condemning the Territories to territorial status forever because it will be unlikely we will be able to obtain the agreement of all the provinces?

I think, Mr. Speaker, there has to come a time when we stop talking in conjecture and speculation and really put some of the things to the test. Considering the fact that there has been a lot of criticism coming from the two Territorial Governments, and from the residents of the North, and that there has been a lot of sympathy from the press and so on, we have to see if in fact this will be really so. The only way to find out whether there would in fact be unanimity or whether one province might not agree, is to not wait and speculate but to go ahead and try it.
I think that many of the provincial premiers, perhaps even the federal Government, are now ready to take into consideration the concerns of the two Territories and the residents of the two Territories in general. So I would wish to have the First Ministers, including the federal Government, look very seriously into what I have suggested, and that is to merge the two, one half of the other territory and the Yukon together. I think that is a very novel thing. I cannot think of why any of the First Ministers would really wish to stop the aspirations of the rest of the population of Canada. If they do, then I would say they deserve all the criticism that has been heaped upon them.
