PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   FRESHWATER FISH MARKETING ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
that Bill C-211, an Act to amend the Freshwater Fish Marketing Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the objective of Bill C-211 is very simple, it is to remove the monopoly presently enjoyed by the Crown corporation, the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation, and allow it to act as a normal fish marketing company would, without the benefit, if that is the right word, of the monopoly. This is not a new idea. It is something I have been pursuing for 15 years, both in the Legislative Assembly of the Northwest Territories and in the House of Commons. Other people were pursuing it long before that, in fact, ever since the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation was set up by statute in Canada in 1969.
The last time this Bill came before Parliament, it was numbered Bill C-235. It was dealt with in June or July, 1985, at which time it was referred to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Oceans and apparently died on the Order Paper of that committee when that session of Parliament came to a close.
In order to understand what we are trying to do here, one has to know a little bit about the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation, how it came into being, where its operations are, and how it conducts its business. It is a federal Crown corporation and operates within the prairie provinces, within the Northwest Territories, and within a small part of Ontario just west of Thunder Bay. It has a head office and principal plant in Transcona, which is just outside the City of Winnipeg.
In 1986, there were total landings of about 45 million pounds of fish, which in general is not a great deal of fish when compared with the East Coast or the West Coast of Canada. The value of that catch, the sales of the corporation in that year, were some $48 million. This information puts it in a kind of context.
When the corporation was established in 1969 it fitted in with the ideology of the day. Shortly after the election of Pierre Elliott Trudeau as Prime Minister of Canada-in the days of the so-called just society-the idea behing it, I guess, was good. It wanted to give the fishermen a better deal. The idea was that instead of having a number of small fish companies trying to sell their fish to American buyers in Chicago and New York, which at that time, and even today, were some of the biggest principal markets for freshwater fish, there would be one organization that would set the terms of trade. However, it did not really work out. The commercial
Freshwater Fish Marketing Act
clout that was supposed to have been given to FFMC never really materialized in fact. Things have gone from bad to worse in the freshwater fish marketing business.
The industry, unfortunately in western Canada, continues to decline, although, and I will get to this later in my presentation, in Ontario where there is a private marketing system, the industry is on the up-ahd-up. Before FFMC came into existence there were a number of relatively small firms in the business, or relatively small, privately-owned firms. There were fishermen, co-operatives, and generally speaking there had been an increase in the amount of fish produced and sold over a number of years until FFMC came into business.
The industry today is hardly what you would call selfsufficient. A number of people describe it as a social industry.
I know in the area that I represent, were it not for something like a 10 cent or 15 cent a pound subsidy given by the territo-fial Government the industry would virtually collapse. That ought not be the case. I am sure it can be a viable industry. It does not have to be looked at as a form of social welfare. It can be a thriving industry that can stand on its own feet.
We have a series of plant closings. That was not suppressed to happen with FFMC, but it does. Over the last few years, on an almost annual or biannual, there are amendments to the FFMC Act which come before Parliament asking for authority to borrow yet more money from the Government of Canada. So it is not really a financially viable operation.
The problem is with Sales. The fishermen know how to catch fish, but what we apparently do not have is somebody who knows how to sell the fish. FFMC has been unable to fulfil its mandate of selling fish. It just does not seem to be able to do it. The last annual report of the company refers to continuing high inventories and the inability to place that fish on the markets. It has resorted to all kinds of techniques to get rid of this supply that is overhanging the market. Sometimes it sells it off at cut-rate prices. It even enters into what I quite frankly think are unlawful agreements to cut down on the supply.
In return for the monopoly the FFMC is supposed to undertake to buy all the fish delivered to it by the fishermen. That was tit for tat. But it is not working out that way. It is putting pressure on fishermen to sign agreements, which I do not think would stand up in a court of law, to restrict the amount of fish to be delivered to the Corporation. Or it can reduce the prices to such a low level that it is just not worthwhile fishing. Or it can close down receiving stations, as it did with the Wool Bay receiving station in my area this summer. There is no place for the fishermen to take their fish, so it can get around the responsabilities that were put onto it by virtue of the Act.
Because of the trouble in the industry a number of studies have been undertaken. I do not know if anybody has any good ideas as to how to make FFMC as it stands work. I do not think they have.

October 1, 1987
Freshwater Fish Marketing Act
The best study, and one of the most recent, on the marketing of freshwater fish in Canada, was the one done by the Standing Senate Committee on Fisheries under the chairmanship of the Hon. Jack Marshall. I would highly recommend it to anyone who wants to know anything about the freshwater fish industry, particularly the marketing aspects thereof, in Canada. It is an excellent document. It makes some good but timorous recommendations. It will not go all the way that is really necessary.
It did recommend, however, a certain degree of private initiative being allowed in the market. Recommendation 13B, which is a rather lengthy one, and I will not read it all into the record, suggest that certain private buyers be licensed and allowed to operate in competition with the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation. That is a good recommendation, one that ought to be put into effect immediately. But in my opinion it does not solve the whole problem. It does not go far enough.
It is interesting to note, Sir, that there is a duplicate freshwater fish marketing system in Canada. We have in the West, including the North, a Crown corporation holding a monopoly where the industry is in decline. On the other hand, in Ontario, which is the other major freshwater fish producing area, we have private enterprise. Anyone is allowed to get into the business of buying and selling fish. There is a free market. This situation would make a wonderful study for professors of economics because here there are two areas in one country. On the one hand there is a socialist system of marketing. On the other hand is a free enterprise system. It is like night and day between them.
In Ontario, the fish business is booming. It cannot keep up with the demand for it. The problem in Ontario is that they are up against the total allowable catch in all these different areas. They cannot get that stuff to market quick enough and in big enough quantities, whereas in the west there are a great number of fish. We never take out the total allowable catch on Great Slave Lake but the problem is that no one can move that fish. They cannot sell it. So it is a wonderful demonstration before our very eyes of the two marketing systems. What I want to do is not to get rid of the FFMC but to revoke that monopoly so that some of those good things that are happening on the Great Lakes of Ontario can also take place in western and northern Canada.
In my opinion, if this Bill is passed into law we will liberate the market, and liberate marketing initiative. FFMC, as I have said before, will continue to exist. But it will have to be competitive. It will have to go out and sell that fish. Fishermen will no longer be at the beck and call of this Crown corporation. They will be able to look around and see if there is somebody else who is willing to pay them a higher price for their product. I do not see that there is anything wrong with that. The fishermen ought to be able to sell the fish that they catch to the people who are prepared to give them the highest price for it.
Although it is not proposed in my Bill, it is quite possible that at some time the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation
will be a candidate for privatization. It is bad enough having a Crown corporation with a monopoly. But it is absolutely unthinkable that a private corporation should have a monopoly. If it is to be privatized in the same manner as Pecheries Canada Incorporated and Fishery Products International Ltd., then the passage of this Bill and the revocation of a monopoly is a required first step.
What type of people are likely to get into the marketing of fish and into competition with FFMC if the business is opened up? Initially, it will not mean direct competition with FFMC. We will see people who are interested in specialty products. One that comes to mind is burbot. That fish is excellent and it makes the best fish and chips that anyone could possibly want to eat. FFMC cannot handle that fish because of Jewish dietary law. If a plant is processing whitefish for the Jewish market, it cannot process burbot, which is a scaleless species, in the same plant. Each year, thousands of pounds of burbot are thrown overboard because FFMC are unable to process that fish. If that market was opened up, private entrepreneurs would be able to handle that particular species in a specialized market.
In my constituency there are certain areas, for example, Great Slave Lake, which produces a high quality product that previously was sold for premium prices, and now it is rolled in with all the other product from Lake Winnipeg and other prairie lakes that FFMC deal with. If the product from Great Slave Lake was dealt with on its own and marketed separately, quite properly a higher price would be received for that particular type of high quality fish. People would initially enter into specialities in species and products, and specialities in areas.
It is likely that fishermen's co-operatives would be revived. They existed in the past, but no longer do. I know a number of fishermen have thought it would be a good idea to get together and form co-operatives to sell their fish. Certain large retailers would also like to be able to buy directly. Lapointe Fish Ltd., a company that has been in Ottawa for many decades, and is a highly reputable fish dealer, would like to be able to buy char directly from fishermen and get it into the stores in Ottawa. Those retailers could pay the fishermen a better price than they are presently receiving from FFMC. In law they are prohibited from doing that. That fish has to go from Baffin Island, to be sold to FFMC in Winnipeg, return to Ottawa, and bear that extra expense. Of course, then the product cannot be sold in Ottawa for a reasonable price. Those are a few of the areas where new people would enter the business.
Efficiency and effectiveness of marketing operations would definitely be increased. There would be much greater over-all marketing effort. As a result, we would end up with larger over-all markets. The Senate study points to vast untapped markets for freshwater fish, particularly in the United States. Markets exist that are much more than we could ever fill. But because of the very limited marketing effort, we are not able to take advantage of that. So there are huge untapped markets out there. With this new marketing effort we could take advantage of them.
October 1, 1987

In my opinion, the end result is that both the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation and the new private or cooperative entrepreneurs would both do better. In that manner, the people who work for FFMC in the plant in Transcona would not be put out of business. There will be an increase in the over-all business and everybody will benefit from that.
In the final analysis, the fishermen, the people that we are worried about, would benefit from higher prices and better returns for their effort.
My final point is why should Canadian citizens be forbidden by law to engage in the honourable profession of fish merchant? Why is that the case? By what right does the Government of Canada prevent anyone from offering a fisherman $2 a pound for his product instead of forcing him to sell it to a government Crown corporation for 20 cents a pound?
I urge all Members to support this Bill, and thereby do justice to the hard-working fishermen of Canada's west and north.

Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure for me to speak on fisheries issues. It is a pleasure that I have had almost yearly during my seven and a half years as a Member of Parliament to speak on the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation.
The Bill that is presented in the name of the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson), Bill C-211, could be entitled "an act to really gut the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation". This is the second time that the Hon. Member for Western Arctic has raised this specific item in Parliament. I refer to his former Bill, Bill C-235, which was debated in the House on June 7, 1985. As the Hon. Member mentioned, it was then referred to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Oceans. The present Bill is no different. The Hon. Member is once again seeking to remove the monopoly provision of the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation.
I must say that I give the Hon. Member much credit for consistency. He has been consistent with his position on this issue since I became a Member of Parliament in 1980. Of course, I cannot say that for all Members of Parliament of the Conservative Party. Certainly, when they became the government that consistency failed.
I am tempted to recall a debate in the House on Private Members' Motions once again on the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation as reported in Hansard on July 10, 1980 at page 2762. I wish to quote from the debate of an Hon. Member who was then in the Opposition and is now on the government side. He stated:
That original concept was recommended by the Mclvor commission in the late sixties and advocated by the Conservative Government of Duff Roblin in the Province of Manitoba. What that concept of a marketing board has become is, as I said a moment ago, a monopolistic, vertically integrated Crown corporation, like so many of our Crown corporations, which handles the product from the lakeside all the way to the consumer, whether the consumer be in the fish buying markets of New York State or Poland.
Freshwater Fish Marketing Act
He went on to say:
I suggest what we have now is a system of monopolistic dominance in the fish marketing industry, in the prairie provinces in particular, which is a far cry from what I understand to be the principle of democratic socialism where free enterprise and the private sector can operate in competition with one another. What we have is virtual communism in all of its forms in the example and illustration of the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation.
Perhaps some Hon. Members will remember who made those comments and may realize what position that particular Member now holds in the House. He now happens to be the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon), so he has all the powers today to do something about it.
I never forgot the debate which occurred in the House on July 10, 1980, because I participated in it. I had never heard such nonsense or such ideological stupidity from a Member of Parliament. I wonder what the Minister has done to reconcile his past convictions with his current responsibility for the corporation.
As I said earlier, the Hon. Member for Western Arctic has been consistent in past debates. I certainly give him credit for that. In a few years from now I suppose writers will be calling the "Mulroney" Government the gang who could not shoot straight. Although the Hon. Member may be a good shot himself, I believe he is shooting at the wrong target today. Very little has happened in the last two years since the Hon. Member spoke on a Bill which, in my opinion, would justify gutting the corporation.
The Hon. Member suggested that the removal of the export monopoly could inject some competition in the prices paid to freshwater fishermen. I am sure all Hon. Members support higher prices for our primary products, but history tells us that the Hon. Member's proposal could do more harm than good.
I certainly support private enterprise in every way possible. In my own riding there is a number of co-operatives which operate very effectively and efficiently. They are owned by the producers and are subject to good management, but when the market is in a downturn, co-operatives suffer as does any other corporation.
I want to comment on the statement of the Hon. Member when he said that there were different species and specialty products for private enterprise. On the surface that is very true, but I would like to refer to what happened when some of my co-operatives were in competition with small private Fish buyers in tough times. If we take lobster as an example, it could be shipped in frozen or raw form to a special market in Toronto, Winnipeg, Vancouver, Montreal, or the United States. They were able to pay fishermen a higher price because they did not have the overhead. However, when fishermen tried to sell smelts, mackerel, or some other species, the cooperative could not pay anywhere near the price and of course did not have the facilities to process the product.

October 1, 1987
Freshwater Fish Marketing Act
The Hon. Member is absolutely correct that certain private enterprises can win on a particular specie or product by having a special market for a special quantity and obtaining a higher price. However, larger co-operatives or companies must sell all fish, all species, or all products produced by fishermen and, therefore, it is an averaging situation.
In the past we have seen, in my province for instance, where some of the fishermen went for the higher price, only to be caught at the end of the day with a specie which they could not sell. Over all they were not better off.
Once again I praise the Hon. Member for his consistency in bringing the matter forward, but he did not comment upon the Senate report on marketing freshwater fish in Canada. It is an excellent report with which I agree.
It is not an easy problem. I know there are isolated areas of the Hon. Member's riding in which some very small plants are located, and that it is very difficult to get fish to the major processing plant and then on to major markets. However, we must average over all for the good of all.
I would ask the Hon. Member to think very seriously about those situations. I know what he wants to do and I appreciate that his will is good. However, I ask him to think seriously before proceeding much further with this Bill, before doing more harm to fishermen than good.
We in the Official Opposition cannot support the Bill in its present form for those reasons.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to make a few remarks about Bill C-211. The Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson), who is sponsoring this piece of legislation, has a number of fishermen in his riding who must deal with the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation.
A minority of the freshwater fishermen in the Northwest Territories, specifically those who are fishing for whitefish, northern pike, and lake trout on Great Slave Lake, are very unhappy about the way in which the corporation operates and markets its fish.
However, we must remember that fishermen in Manitoba, particularly those in northern Manitoba, as well as those in Ontario, Saskatchewan, and Alberta, see the need for the existence of the corporation even though they are not completely satisfied with the way in which it operates at all times. The explanatory note to the Bill indicates that its purpose is to revoke the monopoly which the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation presently has in respect of interprovincial and international sales of such fish. In effect this would eliminate the main function of the corporation. I hope that the Bill was not introduced solely from some ideological desire to dismantle the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation in favour of some form of private enterprise. The Hon. Member said that that was not his intention, but that certainly seems to be the total effect of the Bill.
We need to remember the reason the corporation was established in the first place. It was established because of the failure of private enterprise to sell the catch of freshwater fishermen and because some of these fishermen were in fact being ripped off by some private buyers. These workers needed the support of a marketing agency which was able to expand into alternative markets and to ensure orderly marketing.
The corporation was established in 1969 by the Freshwater Fish Marketing Act for the purpose of marketing and trading in fish and fish products. In the Northwest Territories today more than 300,000 pounds of fish are produced. The corporation has licensed fishermen to sell within the Territories to local businesses, but obviously the market is too small and there is a need to bring the product to outside markets, whether they are provincial ones in Canada or international ones.
Alberta and Saskatchewan have changed their legislation to allow fishermen to sell to other than the final consumer. There is no doubt but that the work of the corporation could be and should be improved. However, most provincial Governments support the concept of a single selling desk operation and would be very leery of any changes which would harm the future incomes of fishermen.
These are some of the changes which need to be looked at. There is a need for more processing to take place in the home community. Fishermen themselves should be given the opportunity to play a more active role and have more control in the running of the corporation. This could be accomplished by having a board of directors with fishermen in the majority. The Senate committee interim report on the freshwater fishery made a number of recommendations for improvements to the marketing board and I would like to highlight some of them.
First, recommendation number five. Because of the high cost of storage, when a surge of fish comes in at a particular time the committee recommends variable pricing be implemented on a large scale to control surges in delivery as well as quality levels. That is already being practised to a limited extent. The fishermen affected should be fully informed of the pricing changes as well as the reason for implementing them.
Recommendation number seven says that a permanent interprovincial freshwater fishery committee composed of provincial and territorial government representatives, corporation representatives, fishermen's elected representatives, and DFO personnel be formed for the purpose of co-ordinating interprovincial fishery policies, sharing information on matters of provincial domain, and taking the responsibility for matters of common concern and common potential benefits. In other words, let us have more territorial and provincial involvement in the operation and a little more co-ordination.
October 1, 1987

Recommendation 13(b), which I think perhaps begins to meet some of the desires of the Hon. Member opposite, suggests that the territorial Government, in co-operation with the federal Government, license a few carefully selected individuals or groups to purchase species from the territorial harvest to be sold in international markets. This would be a pilot project designed to assess whether private enterprise is capable of participating actively in revitalizing the declining fishery of the Territories. The participants must be prepared to market all of their catch. Recommendation 15 is that the corporation and provincial and territorial Governments jointly pursue concerted efforts to stimulate the expansion of the domestic market for freshwater fish.
We recognize that some individuals may not be satisfied with the activities of the corporation. We recognize that some changes are needed. However, what concrete change does this legislation suggest? I am not convinced that the corporation should be stripped of its powers before other mechanisms are put in place. The best interests of all freshwater fishermen must be served, not just a select few of his constituents, so we are unable to give our support to this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I too am interested in speaking to Bill C-221 introduced by my colleague from Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson). However I should like to address the House in the context of the new federal-provincial co-operation era which now prevails in
Canada and praise the positive commitment and the spirit of initiative of the provinces and the Northwest Territories, in cooperation with the federal Government, with respect to the establishment of the Freshwater Fish Marketing Office.
I would express the view that the current market success of the office can be traced back to the federal, provincial and territorial association which led to its establishment.
It has to be a unique association in the history of freshwater fish and, in my estimation, it simply cannot be ignored. I will discuss this historic association in my speech. I intend to support my comments on the unique and dynamic character of this form of co-operation between the federal Government and the provinces with references to an interim report of the Standing Senate Committee on Fisheries, tabled in September 1986.
One of the report's conclusions was that one should not support the centralized marketing system that is the very foundation of the Corporation. The Corporation cannot be considered as an organization that merely carries out the initiatives and objectives of the federal Government. In fact, the history of the Corporation has shown that we have here a model of consultation, co-operation, co-ordination among the six Governments that have an interest in our fresh water fisheries.
As a result of a decision unprecedented in the history of Canada's fisheries, the provincial Governments and the Government of the Northwest Territories decided to concentrate on the problems that were making life terribly difficult for the individual fisherman, and in a show of unity and cooperation, they passed additional legislation to provide for the subsequent establishing of a centralized marketing corporation.
Obviously, unilateral action at a time that has seen significant progress in federal-provincial relations would not only run counter to the very clear signs of co-operation that we are seeing across this country but might also seriously debilitate the fisheries and jeopardize the well-being of our fishermen.
When we say that the Corporation is the result of cooperation by four provinces, the Northwest Territories and the federal Government, it should be added that even before the five Governments passed legislation recognizing that fisheries constitute a specific area that required specific measures, the Government of Manitoba, in a presentation made at a national fisheries conference, stressed that fishermen received only a meager share of constantly fluctuating prices, and that processing and packaging facilities were notorious for poor equipment and poor quality control.
The Manitoba Government added at the time that it knew of no better solution than to create a regional marketing corporation to solve the marketing problems of the industry.
October 1, 1987

It is thanks to such creative leadership on the part of the Governments involved that the Corporation was created. Such an attitude reflects the spirit of federal-provincial co-operation which resulted in a new level of profitability for the freshwater fishing industry and an unprecedented income for the fishermen.
I also wish to underline, Mr. Speaker, that many of the problems, the solving of which was one of the major objectives in setting up the Board and many of which had been identified by the provinces or in the course of the exhaustive study carried out jointly by the provinces and the federal Government, were to a very large extent solved because of the centralized marketing system used by the Corporation.
The problems which had been mentioned by various Members of this House and which had also been the subject of an exhaustive study by the provinces were described after extended consultation with the provinces by Mr. George Mclver in his 1965 report.
He summarized the situation of Canadian fishermen in these terms: They are neither happy nor satisfied, they are very discouraged.
The situation has changed for the better, Mr. Speaker. This remarkable co-operation between the provinces and the federal Government, which is probably still not perfect, has enabled the fishermen to have more influence and to make a profit on the market. The Corporation is a financial success. This success is due partly to the links between six Governments which are at the very source of the sustained and unprecedented record of profitability of the Corporation and the increased income of the fishermen themselves.
The Corporation also succeeded in solving the problems in the industry which had been identified by the provinces. The Corporation has a very good record of taking action to meet the concerns of the provinces and the federal Government. I also believe, Mr. Speaker, that we are fortunate to have such a Corporation at this time and that it will be able to meet the new challenges of the future. Especially since these new and complex challenges were defined by the provinces and more accurately and specifically described by the Standing Senate Committee on Fisheries in September 1986, in its interim report on fresh water fisheries.
These issues are in addition to those concerning pricing and proper marketing procedures previously described by the six Governments.
The very existence of these issues which were dealt with in considerable detail in the report is further proof of the need to continue and refine the work done by the Corporation.
The new situation is self-explanatory, Mr. Speaker. The Corporation is now a financial success and appears to remain
Freshwater Fish Marketing Act
so, bringing prosperity to communities where the fresh water fisheries are a way of life.
The Corporation has just finished the best year it ever had. Last year, total payments to fishermen increased from $28.1 million to $36.6 million, and in an industry that has always been seasonal, it has been possible to maintain sustained growth over the last five years. The provisional report on freshwater fisheries, tabled in September, 1986, by the Senate Standing Committee, despite the apparent success of the Corporation in stabilizing the marketing of Canadian freshwater fish, raises a series of shortcomings that threaten the future of freshwater fisheries. Those dangers relate partly to the forthcoming advent of high techonology in the area of fisheries. Those challenges are just as real as those of an inordinate marketing and the unduly weak share of profits going to fishermen, whose existence has been acknowledged through federal-provincial co-operation.
The new challenges to say the least are more complex than the former ones. They relate to the arrival of capital-intensive technologies and the economic aggravations of product replacement by consumers, as well as the availability of proteinated substitutes on the international market.
1 do not believe fishermen should be the only ones to take up those challenges. That view is shared by the authors of the interim report. They deal especially with the problems, concerns and opportunities in the area of freshwater fisheries, and conclude that it would be more valuable to improve the present system than to replace it outright.
That conclusion is clear. Canadian freshwater fishermen should not be deprived of a protector that has proved to be effective on rapidly changing markets.
In conclusion, I believe that with our provincial counterparts we have forged new ties and written a new page in the history of freshwater fisheries in Canada. Our approach, involving six Governments, and the courage shown by Canadian fishermen have meant success for us on the markets. Therefore, the time is ill-chosen to change the ties that bind us together and to perhaps threaten that co-operation and success in exchange for the uncertain future of a weakened corporation.

EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-NICARAGUA-FUNDING OF CONTRA FORCES BY UNITED STATES/MINISTER'S POSITION
['It being 6.17 p.m., the House stands adjourned until tomorrow morning at 10 a.m. pursuant to Standing Order 3(1).']

Mr. Speaker, on September 17 I asked the Elon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) if he would speak up on behalf of Canada clearly and explicitly and indicate Canadian opposition to any further funding by the United States of America of Contra forces in Nicaragua.
In the past Canada, including the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), has indicated general opposition to foreign intervention in that area and to military funding and so on. However, we have not been specific, we have not specified that the major culprit in that area is the United States which has funded its so-called freedom fighters in Nicaragua who, in fact, are waging a war on development.
When the Prime Minister spoke to a gathering of newspaper people in Vancouver a year ago and indicated this, it received almost no attention in the United States. We spoke too softly. Teddy Roosevelt used to say that America had to speak softly and carry a big stick. Canada does not have a big stick so we should speak up a little more loudly.
That is particularly important at the present time when the five nations of Central America are desperately trying to achieve peace. On August 7 the five nations met in Guatemala and reached a peace accord which calls for such things as an amnesty, a cease fire, the removal of all foreign troops, and the cessation of foreign funding for guerilla movements. When I, along with other people from Canada, including the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), visited Nicaragua in the early part of September as part of the Mission for Peace, we met with a wide variety of people, from Campasinos and co-operatives, up to Vice-President Sergio Ramirez.
Everywhere we went we found that people were tremendously concerned. They wanted peace and were concerned that Nicaragua should meet the conditions of the Guatemala accord. For example, they have appointed the reconciliation commission, at the head of which they placed Cardinal Obando y Bravo who has been one of the most outspoken opponents of the Nicaraguan Government, the Sandinistas. This indicates a real desire to try to bring together the different elements within Nicaragua and meet the peace conditions.
Everywhere we went, people were discussing the question of amnesty for Contras. For example, people in co-operatives were engaged in this debate. We also talked to a group of
mothers who had lost their children in the war. One of them said: "As Christians and as revolutionaries we believe that it is necessary for us to forgive these people and welcome them back into our communities". We heard the same kind of answer at all levels in society.
We saw the re-opening of La Prensa, the newspaper, even at great cost to national security, in accordance with the idea of freedom of the press. Canada would never accept the idea of printing material that could endanger the country's Armed Forces if we were at war.
The major obstacle to achieving peace in Central America is very clear, and has been made clear by everyone to whom we talked. It is the continued funding of the Contras by the United States. We are dealing with an obsession on the part of President Ronald Reagan. He is carrying on a vendetta against the people of Nicaragua and is doing it by funding a group of mercenaries who are not interested in any kind of military encounter with the Army of Nicaragua but in attacking cooperatives, health centres and educational facilities. A school that was built by a group of Canadian volunteers was burned down. A farm funded by ''Farmers For Peace" from Alberta was destroyed by these Contras who were funded by the United States. It is time that Canada speak up along with other countries and indicate that no decent country in the world approves of what President Ronald Reagan is doing and that he is completely isolated in world opinion.
Canada has indicated that it is willing to support the peace process by verification support and perhaps by some help in terms of finances. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has indicated today that he will be going to Central America. That is good and we welcome that kind of initiative. Most important, Canada must speak up and make very clear that the fundamental obstacle to peace in Central America is continued funding of the Contras by the United States and the Reagan administration.
I urge the Government to find the courage to stand up and state that clearly and explicitly.

I know that the Minister shares many of the concerns that have been raised by the Hon. Member and his colleagues, as well as members of the Official Opposition.
When this matter was dealt with in Question Period, the Minister said that he genuinely welcomed the active initiative taken by the Hon. Member, his colleague, and others and this is the reason why he is trying to do whatever will turn out to be practical.
The Hon. Member suggested that the Government of Canada take strong action in this area. I can assure the Hon. Member, through the Secretary of State for External Affairs,
October 1, 1987

that the Government in fact has been doing just that. The Canadian Government's position on Central America has been made very clear on innumerable occasions in the House, in public statements and speeches, to the media and to the various governments involved in the Central American conflicts. We oppose third-party intervention in the region no matter what the source. That includes support for the Contras in Nicaragua.
I would like to point out that the Secretary of State for External Affairs made the Canadian position very clear in his address to the forty-second session of the United Nations General Assembly on September 22. He said:
Canadian aid to the region has been steadily increasing, as has our funding and acceptance of refugees. We have expressed our view that the root problem in Central America is poverty, not ideology; that the real need is development assistance, not military activity; and that intervention by outside powers will only aggravate the tensions. We have supported the Contadora process, and have made available to Contadora the expertise Canadians have acquired in the techniques of peacekeeping.
He went on to say:
Canada supports the initiatives of the Central American Presidents. We are prepared to provide our expertise mechanisms which, once peace is possible, can help it endure.
The disputes must be resolved by those actually involved in the conflict, but Canada is prepared to contribute to that process in any direct and practical way open to us.
The Government of Canada shares the kinds of concerns the Hon. Member has, has taken a strong position on this issue and, I can assure the Hon. Member, will continue to do so.

IMMIGRATION-ARRIVAL OF HONDURANS AT VANCOUVER INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to make some further comments on the question I raised in the House on September 1. At that time I asked the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) if he would consider imposing visa requirements on Hondurans. I was very pleased that in his response he indicated the Government would be prepared to look at this issue and, indeed, on September 18, when I asked if he had a chance to review this matter and had made a decision, he was then able to announce that as of September 18, visa requirements would be in place for Hondurans coming to Canada.
I wanted the chance to make a couple of comments about the story behind this. There has been some misunderstanding about it. Over the past number of months there have been about 1,000 Hondurans come to Canada, the majority of whom have claimed refugee status. Prior to September 18 there had been an increasing number coming to Vancouver on a flight pattern that brought them from Honduras to Mexico City and from Mexico City to Vancouver. Each Thursday a group of approximately 22 Hondurans arrived at Vancouver Airport and indicated they wished to claim refugee status.
It appears that possibly there was a bit of an organized arrangement involved in all this and that a travel agency in the
Adjournment Debate
Honduras had been either aiding or suggesting to people that this would be a way in which they could come to Canada and perhaps gain certain benefits such as being able to work here and resettle here merely by arriving and claiming refugee status. Indeed, it may have been the case that some of these people paid an amount of money to agents to enable them to come to Canada in this manner.
I think it is important, first, that there is no reflection at all on the Hondurans involved. I am sure they are hard working, genuine people who were seeking a better way of life and improved economic conditions. However, it comes back to the basic issue, can we allow our laws to be abused? We are now, fortunately, finally putting in place new laws dealing with refugees to address this kind of situation.
Certainly in my mind and in the mind of my constituents- in fact, in the minds of all Canadians-what we have heard is that they do not want to deny the opportunity to genuine refugees who are fleeing persecution to come to Canada. But they get very angry when they feel that the system is being abused, people are coming here using the guise of the refugee system to gain entry to the country when they should be properly using the regular immigration stream. There are many people who wish to come to Canada. They have to apply, meet the criteria and qualifications. They have to wait in line for that opportunity. So it is not fair that people are using a different way, commonly known as queue-jumping, to get ahead of the line.
I am pleased that the Minister has responded by imposing visa requirements. We all know that visas are not a long-term answer to dealing with this problem. We recognize that they do impose some difficulties for genuine business travellers and tourists who have to go through the extra time and, perhaps, expense of getting a visa before being able to come to Canada. Often that leads to the imposition of visas on Canadians travelling back to the country in question.
Given that Bill C-84 and Bill C-55 have not been completed and given, indeed, the frustration that I think we are all still feeling that Bill C-84, which has been dealt with appropriately in this place, is now going at a very slow pace through the Senate, those tough, new, fair laws are not yet in place. We needed a measure-hopefully only an interim measure-to control the flow of persons from Honduras coming into Canada in an inappropriate manner.
In this respect I am very pleased that the question I asked on September 1 was responded to favourably. The Government took action to address this problem, not only in the specific case of the Hondurans, but it is taking action to address the larger problem of illegal refugees who are trying to come to this country. When we see Bill C-84 and Bill C-55 receive Royal Assent and proclaimed into law, I think many of us will

speakeroldname: Mr. Pat Binns (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subtopic: IMMIGRATION-ARRIVAL OF HONDURANS AT VANCOUVER INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond to the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins) on behalf of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard). When the Hon. Member raised the question a short while ago in Question Period she pointed out, as she has again today, that these Hondurans should be applying through the regular immigration process. Of course, the Minister responded at that time by saying that he was seriously considering imposing a visa requirement in the near future. He went on to say that if the number of arrivals does not decline he will certainly consider the possibility of imposing visa requirements on Hondurans.
The Hon. Member has recognized in her remarks that the Minister has already taken direct action to deal with the concerns which she has raised on behalf of her constituents and on behalf of many, many Canadians. I can only confirm and report the action the Minister has taken. In fact, following consultations with the Department of External Affairs, a visitor visa requirement was imposed on citizens of Honduras effective September 18, 1987.
I would like to emphasize, too, that neither this requirement nor visa requirements in general are implemented for the purpose of preventing genuine refugees from coming to Canada but, rather, to provide the Immigration Commission with the means of deterring bogus refugee claimants from reaching Canadians ports of entry. Of course, this matter of queue-jumping is something which the Government has said it wants to alleviate so that those who go through the regular
channels and follow the regular process will have a fair determination, in turn, following their initial application.
The present refugee determination system permits anyone coming to Canada to make a refugee claim. In fact, we saw that between January 1 and August 30, 1987, 973 Hondurans were reported at Canadian ports of entry as being inadmissible to Canada. As their cases proceed through the immigration system, these persons are likely to make refugee claims.
The inability of the system to quickly distinguish between persons with a potentially valid refugee claim and dispose of those who are in reality economic migrants, coupled with universal access provided by law, has caused our system to be overwhelmed. Increasing numbers of people have recognized that coming to Canada and making a refugee claim can result in an indefinite stay in Canada.
While the number of countries whose citizens require visitor and transit visas has increased, additional problem groups have emerged. Therefore, it has become necessary to impose additional visitor and transit visa requirements in order to prevent the development of a further large backlog of refugee claimants.
In conclusion, I am pleased to report and to confirm that the Minister has taken action, as he indicated to the House he would, in response to the Hon. Member. I am sure that the imposing of visas will accomplish the objective intended by the Minister and the Government.
